verdicts.why: Describes the 'not functioning properly' sense as the plainest member of its family, stays inside the word, negative fits, and the engine example fits this sense.
Blunt, wholesale write-off matches 'not working properly', the contrast with naming an internal fault is a word-level distinction, negative fits, and the telephone-connection example fits.
Fault-carried-inside-the-thing, cooler and more damning than bad, describes this gloss's sense and the word's force; negative fits and the appliance example fits.
Slipped-rather-than-broken tracks 'out of balance or out of adjustment' exactly, 'informal' is a permitted register label, negative is plausible, and the bicycle-wheel example fits.
Purely mechanical, no reflection on the thing, is a fair account of 'having the spring unwound'; neutral fits and the watch example fits this sense rather than the exhausted-person sense.
Covers both halves of the gloss (odor present at all, or a characteristic odor), says the word itself names no particular smell, neutral fits, and all three examples fit this sense.

'Formal' is a register label, the contrast with the family's compounds is a word-form observation not an origin story, and holding onion and garlic together matches the gloss's 'onions or garlic'; neutral is plausible.
Flat identification of the source with no suggestion of welcome is exactly what 'smelling of almond' does; neutral fits.
The licorice-sharp versus softer contrast is only the foil for the point about the word, which is that it names a source and is free of praise or complaint; matches the gloss and neutral fits.
Identifies without evaluating is the word's whole force under 'smelling of apples', the fruit-versus-spice-or-resin placement is a neighbour comparison, and neutral fits.
Balsam itself names the resin, so fixing the smell to the resin rather than the tree is a distinction the word genuinely carries and matches 'smelling of balsam resin'; neutral fits.

Names the smell with no verdict attached is correct for 'smelling of candy' and neutral fits; the made-thing-versus-plant foil is loose (honey and musk are not plants either) but the claim about this word is sound.

The note manufactures a semantic contrast (resemblance versus the source's own smell) out of the gloss saying 'like cedar' where its neighbours say 'of X'; every X-scented compound works by resemblance as readily as by source, so the word does not carry the distinction the note credits it with alone.

The clause 'claimed as the spice's own rather than merely likened to it' asserts that cinnamon-scented encodes real source rather than resemblance, a distinction the word does not make (a cinnamon-scented candle contains no cinnamon); it is the same contrast built from gloss wording as in cedar-scented, seen from the other side.
Passes judgement no more than its neighbour is the correct account of 'smelling of clove', the sharper-spice remark is only a foil for placing it among neighbours, and neutral fits.
Labels a smell by its source without hinting whether it pleases matches 'smelling of ginger' exactly and stays inside the word; neutral fits.
Explicitly separates the source's sweetness from the word's flat reporting, which is the right reading of 'smelling of honey', and the musk-scented comparison is a neighbour contrast; neutral fits.
Neither compound taking a side is the correct account of 'smelling of lemons', the sour-against-sweet pairing with apple-scented is a neighbour comparison, and neutral fits.
